messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rafael's eyes still scan the room with a mix of habit and unease, a reflex honed from years of working as a parole officer in tough neighborhoods. But it wasn't the streets that had finally brought him to therapy – it was the memories he'd been trying to keep at bay since that fateful night five years ago, when his own colleagues turned on him during a routine arrest. The sounds of sirens and shouting still echo in Rafael's mind, but whenever he tries to recall the details, his thoughts are shrouded in an unsettling fog. He pushes the memories away before they can fully form, leaving him with only fragmented images: a baton raised high, the feeling of pavement scraping against his cheek, the weight of a knee on his chest. The more he tries to piece together what happened, the more it feels like a dream – or a nightmare – rather than reality. Rafael's been having trouble sleeping ever since. He wakes up with his heart racing, as if he's still running from those who were supposed to be his brothers in blue. Even during the day, when his own heartbeat pounds in his ears, Rafael feels like he's on high alert, waiting for the other shoe to drop. His wife has noticed it too – how he startles at every little noise, how he constantly scans their surroundings whenever they're out. The triggers are everywhere: a police car driving by, people arguing in public, even the sound of his own heartbeat. For Rafael, each one serves as a reminder that danger lurks around every corner, and that silence can be just as ominous as any shout. He's come to believe that if he'd only been more vigilant, more prepared, maybe things wouldn't have gone so horribly wrong. That sense of failure – or rather, the failure of those who were supposed to protect him – haunts Rafael still. The memory of being left for dead on that pavement, with no one to turn to but the system that had betrayed him, feels like an injustice he can hardly bear. He knows it's eating away at him, making him question his own judgment and trustworthiness as a parole officer. As Rafael recounts these memories in therapy, his voice cracks with emotion – not just from the pain of reliving those moments but also from the knowledge that nothing has been done to hold anyone accountable for what happened. He feels like he's still searching for justice, still seeking vindication for the wounds he received at the hands of those who were sworn to protect and serve. But even as Rafael talks about his desire for closure, his eyes betray a lingering fear – that he'll never be able to shake off the feeling of being on edge, waiting for the next shoe to drop. His wife's gentle touch or a calm conversation with friends might offer temporary respite, but deep down, Rafael knows that until he confronts the memories head-on and finds some measure of peace, he'll remain trapped in this endless cycle of threat and fear. As our sessions draw to a close for the day, Rafael looks around the room once more – not just scanning his surroundings out of habit but also searching for reassurance that he's taking the first steps toward healing. For now, it's a fragile hope, one that flickers like a candle flame in the wind. But with each passing moment, he knows he'll have to confront those memories again, and this time, face the darkness head-on.
